title: Scalable Minimal-Change Learning for Controllable Image Editing

paper.title: Scalable Minimal-Change Learning for Controllable Image Editing
paper.abstract:
Abstract Image editing aims to modify specific attributes of an image while preserving all other aspects. In practice, however, applying even simple editing instructions to existing methods often leads to unintended changes.
We identify the central issue: a fundamental causal principle of minimal change , which requires that an intervention alter only the intended attributes in the output while leaving all others invariant, has not been explicitly incorporated as an optimization objective.
To encourage minimal change, prior work rooted in causal representation learning typically imposes an L 1 L_{1} regularizer on the latent difference between pre- and post-edit representations.
However, this strategy does not scale to modern image editing models: L 1 L_{1} regularization fails to induce true sparsity and instead tends to shrink all latent differences uniformly; sparsity in the latent space does not translate to localized change in the output of nonlinear deep image generation models; and the multi-domain or counterfactual supervision it requires is generally unavailable.
To effectively leverage the minimal change principle for controllable image editing, we cast it as a reinforcement learning objective. Rather than constraining latent representations, we design rewards that directly capture minimal change over intervention outcomes and optimize them explicitly during training.
To produce these rewards reliably, we further introduce an agentic reward model that leverages the chain-of-thought reasoning ability of vision-language models without requiring human annotations. The idea is that instead of emitting a single, unreliable scalar score, the model reasons explicitly about two complementary failure modes, unimplemented changes and unintended changes, and produces this supervision automatically.
Across four benchmarks, ARRO improves average EditScore from 5.21 to 5.88. A region-aware evaluation on 600 examples further shows an 8.4% reduction in off-target pixel change relative to the base editor. Controlled reward and SFT comparisons, blinded human evaluations, and transfer to OmniGen2 provide complementary evidence for the reward design and its applicability beyond one backbone. Code: https://github.com/Showwwwwwwww/ARRO .

Code: https://github.com/Showwwwwwwww/ARRO . 1 Introduction Figure 1: Illustrative edits by FLUX.1 Kontext-dev and Arro . ARRO better preserves the companion, fruit arrangement, umbrella scene, and bus surroundings while carrying out the requested edits. The ambiguous “Include a delicious cake” example remains imperfect: ARRO adds a cake but replaces the original dish. It is retained as a visible failure case rather than evidence of perfect preservation. Image editing aims to modify specific attributes of an image while preserving all other aspects. Recent instruction-based editors ( Brooks et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ; Sheynin et al., 2023 ; Black Forest Labs et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025a ; Wu et al., 2025b ; Deng et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) have made impressive progress on visual quality and instruction following. Yet even simple instructions still trigger widespread, unintended changes: “add glasses” subtly alters the subject’s hair and skin; “change the car’s color” redraws the background; “remove the sign” shifts the lighting of the entire scene. This is not a cosmetic issue but a fundamental one: it determines whether a generative model can be trusted as a controllable editing tool, rather than a high-fidelity sampler that happens to follow instructions most of the time. We identify a central yet under-explored issue behind this gap: the fundamental causal principle of minimal change , which requires that an intervention alter only the intended attributes in the output while leaving all others invariant, has not been explicitly incorporated as an optimization objective in modern image editing models. Minimal change is widely applied in causal representation learning ( Schölkopf et al., 2021 ; Peters et al., 2017 ; Perry et al., 2022 ; Lopez et al., 2023 ) . Existing methods (e.g., ( Yang et al., 2021 ; Shen et al., 2022 ; Komanduri et al., 2022 ) ) operationalize it by imposing an L 1 L_{1} regularizer on the latent difference between pre- and post-intervention representations, encouraging interventions on a single latent factor to leave the remaining factors unchanged. This strategy is difficult to adapt effectively to modern image editing models, due to three obstacles. (O1) L 1 L_{1} does not reliably induce sparsity: it tends to shrink all latent coordinates uniformly toward small values rather than driving most of them to exactly zero ( Shabrina et al., 2025 ) , so latent edits remain dense, just quieter. (O2) Latent sparsity does not translate to output locality: modern decoders are large, deeply nonlinear neural networks with a latent-to-image Jacobian that is far from axis-aligned, so even a sparse change in the latent space can propagate into broad, unintended modifications across the output image ( Shen et al., 2020 ; Karras et al., 2020 ) . (O3) The required supervision does not scale: causal representation learning methods rely on multi-domain datasets with attribute labels or paired counterfactual examples, which are expensive or generally unavailable. We address all three obstacles by reformulating minimal change as a reinforcement learning (RL) objective on intervention outcomes rather than latents. Designing rewards that directly capture minimal change on the output dissolves (O1) and (O2) simultaneously: there is no L 1 L_{1} approximation to optimize, and the decoder’s nonlinearity is no longer a problem, because the reward is computed directly on the output rather than on the latent that produces it. Concretely, the supervised dataset contains only source-instruction pairs ( 𝒙 src , c ) (\bm{x}_{\text{src}},\,c) ; during RL, the current policy samples candidate edits 𝒙 i \bm{x}_{i} , which are then assigned minimal-change rewards r i r_{i} according to how well they implement the instruction while leaving everything else intact. To address (O3) , a minimal-change reward has to be reliably designed without human annotation. A natural choice would be to ask a vision-language model (VLM) for a single editing quality score, as in recent reward-modeling work ( Gong et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2025 ) . However, directly prompting a VLM for a numerical score is unreliable. First, the score is poorly calibrated: scalar VLM ratings are noisy and high-variance, with thresholds that shift across images, so the same numerical score can mean different things on different inputs ( Li et al., 2026 ) . Second, the score is uninformative about the type of failure: a minimal-change reward must capture two distinct aspects, whether the instructed edit was carried out and whether everything else was left alone, but a single number collapses both into one signal, so the policy cannot tell which aspect it is failing on. To make the minimal-change reward more reliable, we design an agentic reward model: rather than asking the VLM for a numerical score, we leverage its chain-of-thought reasoning ability to perform a structured audit of the edit. We decompose the minimal-change reward into two complementary components: unimplemented changes , where the instructed edit is missing or incomplete, and unintended changes , where modifications appear outside the instructed scope. For each component, the VLM reasons over the editing triplet of source image, instruction, and edited output, and produces a list of identified issues. To stabilize the agentic reward model, we further introduce a rubric refinement loop that enforces consistency within each GDPO group (the set of candidate edits sampled for a given source-instruction pair). An LLM first merges the candidates’ audit lists into a single deduplicated rubric. The VLM then performs a second-pass evaluation in which, for each candidate, it selects the applicable items from this shared rubric, and the two reward signals are computed from the selected items. On top of FLUX.1 Kontext, our method lifts average EditScore from 5.21 5.21 to 5.88 5.88 across four benchmarks (MinEval, MagicBrush, AnyBench, and Emu-Edit). A masked pixel-difference evaluation on 600 examples measures 8.4% less off-target change than the base editor. Under fixed GDPO training, replacing ARRO’s rewards with EditScore Prompt-Following and Consistency rewards yields 3.78 3.78 average EditScore, while ARRO achieves 5.88 5.88 . On MinEval, ARRO-GDPO also exceeds reward-guided Top-10 SFT ( 5.669 5.669 vs. 4.629 4.629 EditScore). Blinded human comparisons and transfer to OmniGen2 provide further evidence. These results support supervising the effect of an intervention. Contributions. (1) We diagnose three reasons why latent-space sparsity fails to deliver minimal change in modern generative editors ineffective L 1 L_{1} regularization, decoder nonlinearity, and the lack of scalable supervision and recast minimal change as a reinforcement learning objective on intervention outcomes, optimized end-to-end over a flow-matching editor. (2) We design an agentic reward model that, unlike scalar VLM judges, reasons over the editing triplet to produce decomposed efficacy and locality rewards from raw images alone counting unimplemented and unintended changes, respectively stabilized by a group-level rubric refinement step that anchors all candidates to a shared, deduplicated set of canonical issues. (3) We developed MinEval, a dataset of automatically generated edit prompts and source images covering atomic changes across six edit types, with disjoint training and held-out evaluation splits. MinEval is designed to facilitate research into controllable image editing. (4) On top of FLUX.1 Kontext, Arro improves average EditScore from 5.21 5.21 to 5.88 5.88 across four benchmarks and reduces masked off-target pixel change by 8.4% on a 600-example evaluation. Reward-pipeline, EditScore-reward, and Top-10 SFT controls, human evaluations, and OmniGen2 transfer probe the source and breadth of these gains (Sec. 4 ; App. C.1 ). 2 Related Work Instruction-based Image Editing. Following Brooks et al. (2023) , recent models like FLUX.1 Kontext ( Black Forest Labs et al., 2025 ) treat locality as an emergent property of pretraining. However, unintended background drift persists in current benchmarks ( Qian et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ) . Post-training approaches address this via preference optimization ( Wallace et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ) or online RL ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ) using learned reward models ( Luo et al., 2025 ; Gong et al., 2025 ) . We depart from this line in two ways: (1) we argue human preference rewards often conflate aesthetics with adherence rather than penalizing non-minimal changes, and (2) our agentic VLM reward is zero-shot, bypassing the need for expensive, learned reward-model training. Flow Matching and Sampling Efficiency. Research on generative flow matching has improved few-step synthesis through model-aligned training couplings ( Lin et al., 2025b ) and sub-mode conditioning for diverse one-step generation ( Lin et al., 2026 ) .
